content_voiceover: This slide distills primary hemostasis into two discrete steps, adherence and aggregation. Adherence happens first, platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX complex binds von Willebrand factor that's anchored to the exposed subendothelium, tethering the platelet to the injury site. Aggregation happens next, activated platelets express glycoprotein IIb-IIIa, which binds fibrinogen, and because fibrinogen is a bivalent molecule, it bridges adjacent platelets together, building the platelet plug. This two-receptor model is a favorite board framework because each step maps to a distinct bleeding disorder. Loss of GP Ib-IX function or expression causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, which classically presents with giant platelets and thrombocytopenia on smear. Loss of GPIIb-IIIa causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which presents with a normal platelet count and normal size but a flat aggregation response to essentially all agonists except ristocetin.
keypoints: Adherence: platelet GP Ib/IX binds VWF on subendothelium
Aggregation: platelet GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, bridges platelets
GP Ib/IX defect → Bernard-Soulier (giant platelets, thrombocytopenia)
GPIIb/IIIa defect → Glanzmann thrombasthenia (normal count, poor aggregation)
keypoint_voiceover: Memorize this pairing cold for boards. GP Ib-IX plus VWF equals adherence, and its defect is Bernard-Soulier syndrome with giant platelets and thrombocytopenia. GPIIb-IIIa plus fibrinogen equals aggregation, and its defect is Glanzmann thrombasthenia, with a normal platelet count but absent aggregation to agonists other than ristocetin.
